first_reader_source: PDF of the NIST author manuscript
title: Beyond fentanyl test strips: Investigating other urine drug test strips for drug checking applications

claims.statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read by site staff, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco et al. (2024b): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL.

claims.statement: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips of different brands, production lots and ages did not perform the same, compared with the known content of prepared solutions. Lots: in one laboratory, two lots of one brand (BTNX Rapid Response, urine cut-off 20 ng/mL) obtained in 2017 detected fentanyl in water down to 20 ng/mL, while three lots obtained in 2021 detected it only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher, and in urine, the strips' intended use, down to 50–100 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also gave false positives with lidocaine, MDMA and diphenhydramine at concentrations 10 to 200 times lower, and with d-methamphetamine at a twofold higher one (editors' calculation on the study card). The two sets were tested in separate rounds (2017 and 2022), with storage and expiry not reported, so lot, storage and testing round cannot be separated (Halifax et al., 2024). Brands: on the same solutions, four brands detected 5 to 12 of 23 analogues at 100 ng/mL; one brand (One Step) read negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at every concentration, which the other three detected at higher concentrations, and it alone gave false positives with ascorbic acid at 10 mg/mL or more (Bergh et al., 2021). Heat and age: strips with a listed cut-off of 200 ng/mL detected 500 ng/mL whether or not they had been kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks; strips of an older lot more than four years past expiry, kept in laboratory conditions, detected 250 ng/mL against their listed cut-off of 20 ng/mL, which is not less sensitive than the in-date strips in absolute terms (editors' comparison; Sisco et al., 2024b, one lot each, triplicates). In another laboratory, every strip in diphenhydramine solutions at 4 °C read positive at all three concentrations tried, with no fentanyl-free cold solution tested (Lockwood et al., 2021). How strips perform after storage as people keep them, after longer heat, or across many lots and brands was not measured. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Halifax et al.: fentanyl in water 20 ng/mL (2017 lots) against 200 ng/mL (2021 lots); in urine 50 and 100 ng/mL (2021 lots); false-positive thresholds 2017 against 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 5 against 10, MDMA 50 against 2.5–5, lidocaine 100 against 2.5, diphenhydramine 100 against 0.5–1 mg/mL. Bergh et al.: analogues at 100 ng/mL 5, 5, 12 and 9 of 23 by brand; One Step negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at all concentrations; ascorbic acid false positives on One Step only. Sisco et al. (2024b): fentanyl strips 0.5 µg/mL heated or not (listed 0.2 µg/mL); expired fentanyl strips 0.25 µg/mL (listed 0.02 µg/mL); expired methamphetamine strips 5 against 1 µg/mL; expired cocaine strips unchanged at 2.5 µg/mL. Lockwood et al.: at 4 °C all diphenhydramine strips positive at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL.

claims.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands and production lots. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone (Green et al., 2020). Drug-checking data from British Columbia, known only second-hand, point the same way: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al.); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration (Lockwood et al., 2021); a positive reading at 100 ng/mL on all four brands tested, though two showed only a barely visible test band there, which the makers' rule (any visible band means negative) would read as negative (Bergh et al., 2021, single readings); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b), a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), the seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation). Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al.); 25 ng/mL by eye (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024).

claims.statement: In laboratory tests of the first commercial nitazene test strip (BTNX Rapid Response; maker's cut-off 2000 ng/mL isotonitazene) on pure nitazene standards in water and on nearly pure seized powders, compared with known content, the strips detected most nitazenes tested but missed one group entirely. Read from photographs by two blinded raters and by image analysis, isotonitazene read positive in all six replicates from 3000 ng/mL with one lot and 2000 ng/mL with another, obtained about four months apart. With one lot and one strip per concentration, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues read positive at 9000 ng/mL or less; nine did not at 9000 ng/mL: the six desnitazenes, which lack the 5-nitro group (among them metodesnitazene and etodesnitazene), 5-aminoisotonitazene and two analogues with a longer link between the rings. Six seized powders, each estimated as more than 90% one nitazene, all read positive at about 1 and 0.1 mg/mL (6 of 6; editors' Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%) (De Vrieze et al., 2024). In a second laboratory, the strips detected metonitazene from 1 µg/mL and N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene from 5 µg/mL (ten strips per level), and reacted to none of 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds at two concentrations (Sisco et al., 2024b). No study read tested nitazene-free street samples or mixtures in which a nitazene is a small part of heroin, other opioids or stimulants, so how often the strips miss nitazenes or give false positives in real samples is unknown; preliminary street-sample figures cited from the maker's material (12 samples) are unpublished. The first study's authors write that a negative result does not mean a sample is free of nitazenes or safe, and that a positive one does not show which nitazene is present or how much. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: De Vrieze et al.: isotonitazene limit (all six replicates positive) 3000 ng/mL (lot A) and 2000 ng/mL (lot B), the same by visual and image-analysis scoring; analogues (lot B, single strips) 24 of 33 positive at 9000 ng/mL or less (visually 16 at 1000 and 3000 ng/mL, 7 at 3000 ng/mL only, 1 at 9000 ng/mL only), 9 not detected at 9000 ng/mL; powders 6 of 6 positive at both concentrations (Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%, editors' calculation on the card). Sisco et al. (2024b): limits 1 µg/mL (metonitazene) and 5 µg/mL (N-piperidinyl etonitazene, protonitazene); no reaction with 76 non-nitazene compounds at 0.01 and 0.5 or 1 mg/mL.

claims.statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, detected xylazine reliably when there was at least the strip's listed amount and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not, so these strips would not show them (Sisco et al., 2024a). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Sisco et al. (2024a), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL: lidocaine only of 76 other compounds. Sisco et al. (2024b), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.
